title: The Postcard of Junebug Creek
premise: Isandro Blackwood ghostwrote the memoirs of Judge Corliss Vance, the man whose testimony destroyed his family twenty years ago, hiding his identity behind a professional mask. When a postcard mailed eleven years ago from Junebug Creek finally reaches him, it reveals that Vance's celebrated verdict was built on perjury — and that the woman Isandro loved and abandoned, Marisol Reyes, was the one who tried to tell him. Returning to Junebug Creek under cover of finishing Vance's book, Isandro finds Marisol fighting to reopen the case before the statute closes it forever, and discovers the love he buried never died. As Vance's power closes around them both, Isandro must choose between exposing himself as the memoir's true author — destroying his career and safety — or letting injustice stand; in the end he testifies, Marisol's brother is freed, and Isandro stays past the last train, choosing her over the life he built to hide.
about_author: Hazel Thackeray is the pen name of a former small-town court reporter who spent a decade transcribing other people's justice before writing her own. She lives near a creek she refuses to name, where she writes novels about the cost of staying silent.

chapters.title: The Weight of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In Chicago, Isandro finishes ghostwriting Judge Corliss Vance's triumphant memoir, invisible as always, paid well to disappear into another man's voice. A routine archive request surfaces an unclaimed postcard addressed to him, postmarked eleven years ago from Junebug Creek. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Eleven Years Late
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He reads Marisol's postcard: 'They lied at the trial. Come before the trains stop running.' The handwriting undoes twenty years of careful distance. He tells himself it's too late, then books a ticket anyway. Beat: the safe life cracks open.

chapters.title: Junebug Creek
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The town has decayed since he fled it at nineteen; the depot is scheduled for demolition, the last train leaving in six weeks. He checks into a boarding house under his pen-name identity. Beat: homecoming as trespass.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Records Office
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol, now the county's records clerk, has spent eleven years quietly pulling files on her brother Teo's wrongful conviction — the trial where young Isandro testified against him. She doesn't know Isandro is back. Beat: righteous exhaustion, hope worn thin.

chapters.title: A Ghost in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds someone has requested the same trial transcripts she's been copying for years. The signature is unfamiliar; the handwriting isn't. She recognizes Isandro's slanted 'r' from old letters. Beat: suspicion sharpening into recognition.

chapters.title: Coffee, Cold
chapters.summary: Dual POV. They meet at the diner, circling each other with eleven years of unfinished sentences between them. Isandro claims he's here to finish Vance's book; Marisol lets him believe she believes him. Beat: love and war wearing the same face.

chapters.title: What the Judge Built
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Researching Vance's memoir chapters, Isandro cross-references the trial record and finds the timeline impossible: the witness who placed Teo at the scene couldn't have been there. Vance coached the lie. Beat: horror of realizing his own testimony was the keystone.

chapters.title: Teo
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Visiting Teo in state prison, Marisol shares her findings; he begs her to stop — Vance's people have threatened her before, and their mother died waiting. Beat: love against duty, duty winning for now.

chapters.title: The Boarding House Confession
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. His landlady, Mrs. Okonkwo, remembers the trial and the Blackwood family scandal; she knows who he is and says nothing, only leaves him his mother's old recipe for supper. Beat: unexpected grace; the town forgiving what he can't forgive himself.

chapters.title: Vance Arrives
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Judge Vance sweeps into town to promote his memoir, trailed by aides and a fixer named Dell Harrow. He treats Isandro warmly as 'my writer,' a leash disguised as affection. Beat: power entering the room like weather.

chapters.title: The Archive Fire
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A fire guts the county annex overnight; the original trial evidence burns. Marisol had checked out the key box two days earlier — the only surviving copy is hidden in her floorboards. Beat: terror and resolve; the enemy is real and close.

chapters.title: Allies in the Dark
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Isandro confronts Marisol about the fire; cornered, they finally trade truths — his coerced testimony, her brother's innocence, the postcard lost in a dead letter office for a decade. They agree to work together. Beat: alliance becoming intimacy.

chapters.title: What We Were Before
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Walking the creek at dusk, they remember being eighteen — the summer before the trial tore everything apart. An almost-kiss breaks off when Harrow's car passes slowly. Beat: tenderness shadowed by surveillance.

chapters.title: The Fixer's Offer
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Harrow offers Isandro money and a prestigious byline to hand over whatever Marisol has and leave town. Isandro refuses, but realizes Vance now suspects his identity. Beat: temptation refused, danger doubled.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Testimony
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The landlady comes forward: she saw the real perpetrator near the rail yard the night of the crime, and was paid to forget. Her statement gives them a living witness. Beat: ordinary courage tipping the scale.

chapters.title: Deadline: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The depot demolition moves up; the final train leaves in nine days, and the appellate filing must reach the capital by then or the window closes forever. They race to authenticate documents. Beat: clock ticking loud enough to hear.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Margins
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Harrow reveals he's read Isandro's draft notes — proof Isandro knew the verdict was false and wrote Vance's legend anyway. Blackmail: testify for Teo and be exposed as complicit, or stay silent and keep his name clean. Beat: the trap of his own complicity.

chapters.title: The Longest Night
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol learns of the blackmail and, hurt, nearly walks away — until she finds Isandro at 3 a.m. drafting a public confession, career and all. She stays. Beat: love chosen not despite the wreckage but inside it.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At the emergency evidentiary hearing, Isandro takes the stand, names himself, recants his childhood testimony, and presents the burned-case survivor documents. Vance unravels on cross-examination. Beat: climax — truth spoken at maximum personal cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Teo's conviction is vacated; Vance resigns under federal investigation; Harrow cuts a deal. Isandro's exposure ends his ghostwriting career — and, strangely, frees him. Beat: justice outside the law's timetable, finally inside it.

chapters.title: The Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the condemned depot, the final train pulls out without Isandro aboard. He watches it go, holding nothing but a return ticket he'll never use. Beat: letting the escape route go.

chapters.title: Stay
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, closing on both. Weeks later, Isandro writes his first book under his own name — the true story of Junebug Creek — while Marisol pins his old postcard above the records office desk, answered at last. Beat: resolution; a life measured no longer in safe steps but in stayed ones.
